Graph overlays on an iris UMAP

Source: vignettes/articles/graph-overlays.Rmd
graph-overlays.Rmd

In the iris UMAP below, setosa forms a group of its own. Versicolor and virginica run together. To see which flowers link those two species, we can take the edges from uwot’s fitted graph and draw them over the points. Click any static plot for a closer look.

Fitting UMAP to iris

The four numeric columns of iris go into UMAP. The two extras worth keeping here are the ranked neighbors (ret_nn = TRUE) and the fitted fuzzy graph (ret_extra = "fgraph"). All the plots below use one saved run of this code.

X <- as.matrix(iris[, 1:4])
set.seed(65)
fit <- uwot::umap(
  X,
  n_neighbors = 15,
  n_threads = 1,
  ret_nn = TRUE,
  ret_extra = "fgraph"
)
library(vizier)

xy <- fit$embedding
species <- iris$Species
palette <- c(setosa = "#0072B2", versicolor = "#D55E00", virginica = "#009E73")
edges <- embed_edges(fit$fgraph)
#> Loading required namespace: Matrix
between <- subset(edges, species[from] != species[to])

Edges between species

The fitted graph is symmetric, so embed_edges() takes its upper triangle. We get one row per pair, with the membership strength in weight. The from and to columns are row numbers in iris, so species[from] != species[to] picks out the edges between different species. The iris rows happen to be sorted by species, which is why the counts fall on one side of the table.

with(between, table(species[from], species[to]))
#>             
#>              setosa versicolor virginica
#>   setosa          0          0         0
#>   versicolor      0          0        97
#>   virginica       0          0         0
map <- function(overlay = NULL) {
  embed_ggplot(
    xy,
    species,
    overlays = overlay,
    cex = 0.8,
    color_scheme = palette,
    fixed_aspect = TRUE
  ) +
    ggplot2::theme_classic() +
    ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}
map() + ggplot2::labs(title = "Species", colour = NULL)
map(between) + ggplot2::labs(title = "Cross-species edges", colour = NULL)

In this fit, all 97 cross-species edges join versicolor to virginica. Setosa has no fitted edge to either species.

Keeping one neighbor per flower

A quick way to thin out the plot is to keep one neighbor per flower. fit$nn[[1]] lists the neighbors from the four original measurements in order of distance. The first panel below uses the nearest neighbor in that list and the second uses the furthest. embed_edges() skips the flower itself by row ID, so a different flower at zero distance still counts. Two flowers can choose each other, which is why count_bridges() counts each pair only once.

nn <- fit$nn[[1]]
nearest <- embed_edges(nn, select = "nearest")
furthest <- embed_edges(nn, select = "furthest")
views <- list(Nearest = nearest, Furthest = furthest, Fitted = edges)

count_bridges <- function(e) {
  cross <- e[species[e$from] != species[e$to], , drop = FALSE]
  nrow(unique(data.frame(
    a = pmin(cross$from, cross$to),
    b = pmax(cross$from, cross$to)
  )))
}
counts <- vapply(views, count_bridges, integer(1))
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(1, 1, 3, 1), lwd = 1.25)
for (name in names(views)) {
  embed_plot(
    xy,
    species,
    overlays = views[[name]],
    cex = 0.8,
    color_scheme = palette,
    fixed_aspect = TRUE,
    show_axes = FALSE,
    title = sprintf("%s\n%d cross-species pairs", name, counts[[name]])
  )
}

Keeping the nearest neighbor gives 5 distinct cross-species pairs. Keeping the furthest gives 11. Either way, we miss plenty of connections in the fitted graph. To pick the tenth neighbor specifically, use embed_edges(nn, select = "furthest", k = 10).

Neighbor preservation in 2D

quadra is an R package for measuring how well an embedding preserves the structure of the original data. Install it from GitHub with pak::pak("jlmelville/quadra") (run install.packages("pak") first if you need pak).

Of a flower’s ten nearest neighbors in the original measurements, how many are still among its ten nearest neighbors on the map? quadra::nn_preservation() gives us the fraction retained for each flower. A score of 0.7 means seven flowers appear in both lists.

quality <- quadra::nn_preservation(
  X,
  xy,
  k = 10,
  nn_method_in = "brute",
  metric_in = "euclidean",
  metric_out = "euclidean",
  ret_extra = TRUE
)
retained <- quality$nnpv$nnp10

Hover over a flower for its row number, species and score. Click it to draw its edges, then click another flower to switch. You can see more than ten lines on a click because the lines show every edge uwot fitted to that flower. The color comes from quadra’s ten-neighbor calculation above.

embed_plotly(
  xy,
  retained,
  overlays = list(edges = edges, mode = "incident"),
  limits = c(0, 1),
  color_scheme = "grDevices::Viridis",
  fixed_aspect = TRUE,
  tooltip = sprintf(
    "%s | %d of 10 neighbors retained",
    species,
    round(10 * retained)
  )
)

The mean fraction retained here is 0.71. If you’re only interested in connections between species, change edges = edges to edges = between. Clicking a flower with no cross-species edges then clears the lines.

Bundling the fitted graph

With all the edges drawn, the straight lines pile up around some of the flowers. In the right panel below we’ll bundle the edges and give the stronger ones more ink. Membership weight maps linearly to opacity, from 0.01 at weight 0 to 0.25 at weight 1. prepare_overlay() computes the Hammer paths once. For a larger graph, add n_threads = 4L to the specification to use up to four threads during preparation.

weighted_hammer <- list(
  edges = edges,
  route = "hammer",
  alpha = "weight",
  alpha_limits = c(0, 1),
  alpha_range = c(0.01, 0.25)
)
hammer <- prepare_overlay(xy, weighted_hammer)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 3, 1), lwd = 1.25)
embed_plot(
  xy,
  retained,
  overlays = edges,
  limits = c(0, 1),
  color_scheme = "grDevices::Viridis",
  fixed_aspect = TRUE,
  show_axes = FALSE,
  cex = 0.8,
  title = "Straight edges"
)
embed_plot(
  xy,
  retained,
  overlays = hammer,
  limits = c(0, 1),
  color_scheme = "grDevices::Viridis",
  fixed_aspect = TRUE,
  show_axes = FALSE,
  cex = 0.8,
  title = "Weighted Hammer paths"
)

Both panels connect the same 1,347 pairs. In the right panel, nearby paths bend together and weaker edges fade. A curve can pass close to a third flower on its way between the two flowers it actually connects.

embed_ggplot() can use hammer as it stands, with the same paths and continuous edge opacity. The colorbar shows the fraction of neighbors each flower kept.

embed_ggplot(
  xy,
  retained,
  overlays = hammer,
  cex = 0.8,
  limits = c(0, 1),
  color_scheme = "grDevices::Viridis",
  fixed_aspect = TRUE
) +
  ggplot2::theme_classic() +
  ggplot2::labs(colour = "Fraction retained")

Plotly uses one line trace per distinct opacity. With continuous opacity, we’d need 1,208 traces for this graph. Set alpha_bins = 4L on a copy of hammer and each path gets the nearest of four opacities (0.01, 0.09, 0.17 and 0.25). Now Plotly can draw the graph in four traces. It still gets every sampled point along each path, and we can still hover over a flower to read its score.

hammer_plotly <- hammer
hammer_plotly$alpha_bins <- 4L
embed_plotly(
  xy,
  retained,
  overlays = hammer_plotly,
  limits = c(0, 1),
  color_scheme = "grDevices::Viridis",
  fixed_aspect = TRUE,
  tooltip = sprintf(
    "%s | %d of 10 neighbors retained",
    species,
    round(10 * retained)
  )
)
